title: Super fund chiefs defend Firmus IPO snub as ‘doing their job’
full_text:
One of the country’s top superannuation funds’ chief investment decision makers has described investors not choosing to back the $7bn Firmus initial public offering as an example of them doing their job.
The comments were made by Aware Super chief investment officer Simon Warner on a panel at the Citi Australia and New Zealand investment conference in Sydney.
They come not only weeks after the IPO of Firmus – one that would have been one of the largest in Australia – failed to happen, and on the same day as another more established artificial intelligence bet, Next DC, saw its shares crash 40 per cent on the back of a major earnings downgrade by the data centre operator.
“Firmus is an example of investors doing their job,” Mr Warner said when commenting on the lack of support from the Australian investment community for the $7bn IPO plan.
“We are now in a phase of investors doing their job and we have an obligation to pick and choose where you deploy capital.”
Investors baulked at not just the $44bn market value but the lack of fundamentals around the data-centre operator and developer.
Australian super funds shunned the deal and UniSuper chief investment officer John Pearce, who was also on the Citi panel, has made it known that the fund that oversees about $175bn of superannuation assets under management would not be investing in Firmus because it was too speculative.
Mr Pearce said apart from Goodman Group, in which UniSuper had an overweight investment, it was not an investor in data centres.
“We understand that there are a lot of adjacencies,” he said in connection to the AI boom, for which he said was at the start rather than mid-cycle.
“The big winners are still to come.”
Aware Super is Australia’s third largest super fund with $240bn under management.
Mr Warner pointed out that data centres were so diverse and investment decisions around them were a lot more detailed than they used to be.
He said old data centres are now unable to take the chips, which begged the question: how were those sites repurposed?
The question was being raised by Mr Warner as investors in the $4bn NextDC were asking questions of their own, such as does the company now become a takeover target of the Nasdaq-listed rival Equinix after shedding 40 per cent of its value?
The $US100bn Equinix has eyed NextDC before, as have private equity funds like Brookfield, Blackstone and EQT.
Sources believe it would be just a matter of time before it became a target, but most think suitors would wait for the dust to settle following NextDC’s news.
It said it had revised its net revenue and earnings and capital spending guidance for the year ending June 30 2027 due to delays to electricity network works by Jemena, impacting grid supply to its M3 Melbourne data centre delivery.
Revenue for fiscal 2027 had been revised to $475m to $500m from $615m to $640m and underlying earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation was revised to between $245m and $265m from $385m to $410m.
Compounding weak sentiment for AI and data centre hopefuls has been the 30 per cent decline in the AI neocloud provider CoreWeave in the past month.
The Wall Street Journal reported that AI cloud-computing company Elice’s shares shed as much as 36 per cent from their IPO price in their South Korean trading debut.
Bloomberg reports that DayOne Data Centers is weighing options for its US initial public offering, including a potential delay or size cut, as volatility around data centres increases.
